New CitizenCentral portal in testing, to be launched later this year.

A new way for ratepayers in Waitaki to pay their rates, register their dogs, and log enquiries and requests with Council has been shortlisted for the Association of Local Government Information Management (ALGIM) project of the year award.

CitizenCentral is a customer-focused portal which ties in with Council’s existing digital infrastructure, allowing greater on-demand access to a range of Council’s services.

In just three months, the project team has set up;

• Complete 24/7 access including payment status, history, and outstanding balances.
• Integrated platform for rates, water, and infringement payments, creating and reviewing
• service requests, progress tracking, and updating citizen details.
• Multi-ratepayer payment capability from any location
• Future-ready animal registration system

The best part? The cost for this is under $30,000 – clocking in at $29,115. Instead of the expensive replacing of an entire system, this makes better use of what already works – and gives the community 24/7 access to online services.

Waitaki District Council is the first council in New Zealand to implement CitizenCentral, as part of its commitment to being a leading, innovative Council which delivers the best for the community.

CitizenCentral is the product of the new operating model for Council, bringing together Customer Services, Digital Services and the team responsible for Council’s transformation programme.

The portal itself is currently being tested by a selected group of community members, before a fuller public rollout later this year.

As Oamaru Airports first ever full-time manager, Matt Sisson has spent his first month in the role getting to know the country’s sixth busiest airport for plane movements. 

“I don’t think people understand just how many aircraft are on the move just north of town these days” he said, “The idea that Oamaru is a sleepy little airport is definitely not the reality once you get airside. That presents challenges, and the most important one is how the airport grows sustainably and safely in the future”

With more than 14 years’ experience as an aircraft engineer at Air New Zealand, he’s no stranger to the aviation world. That hands-on technical background naturally led him into managing Airport Operations and Safety at Timaru and Hokitika Airports, where he focused on keeping things running smoothly and safely for both staff and travelers.

Matt brings close to 10 years of experience in construction project management — including leading the apron extension and runway reseal at Timaru Airport. His mix of aviation and project work means he’s got a sharp eye for detail, a strong sense of the big picture, and a practical, solution-focused mindset.

Ensuring the current runway surface life extends to the 2027/28 financial year, when the Long-Term Plan budget allocates funding for resurfacing, is also a priority.

“My role is to manage the airport, meet all of the safety and regulatory requirements and ensure that the assets owned by Council meet the planning and budgetary needs set by the Mayor and Councillors.”

Speaking about the appointment, Council Chief Executive, Alex Parmley said:

“Oamaru airport is a fantastic asset for our district and our local economy and it has grown immensely over recent years. This means there is more to do to ensure the airport runs safely, and that it is well managed and maintained, particularly with this increased use. Carrying on the way we were was not an option and we knew we needed an aviation professional with a community focus and a collaborative approach to help us manage the airport and make improvements.”

“It is great to welcome Matt to Waitaki. He’s genuinely passionate about the aviation industry and is looking forward to working alongside Council teams and the users of the airport to help deliver a safe, efficient, and community-friendly airport environment.”

Not with the Kakanui Bridge replacement.

Waitaki District Council is mid-way through replacing the 126-year-old Kakanui Bridge. Four of its piers are now in place, with two more being installed in the coming weeks. The first of the 42 bridge beams were also delivered to site this week.

This is a State Highway 1 resilience route, and by reducing the piers in the water from 15 to just 6, and raising the height of the bridge, it's designed to handle high-river flows and reduce the issues that slash buildup cause on the existing bridge.

The old bridge will be deconstructed once the new one opens, and while it's a beloved part of Kakanui - it has reached the end of its use-life (and beaten its anticipated lifespan by over a quarter century!) A new boat ramp will be built where the old bridge connects to the west bank of the Kakanui River.

Last week Waitaki District Council’s Governance Team approved the new Council brand design. You might have noticed our logo change this week on this and other platforms.

The Waitaki District Council brand was last updated in 2013.

This refresh also coincides with Council’s transformation into a more rationally organized, cost effective and efficient organisation – to ensure Waitaki District Council is a leading, innovative council delivering the best for our communities.

The change will be digital-first, updating assets and logos and colour palletes across our increasing online offering. Offline, we’ll be renewing signage, uniforms and fleet as part of the existing budgets for replacement.

We’re also mindful of the fiscal environment, and the brand was developed in-house by our talented team. We’ve attached some more information about the evolution of our brand, and the new logo, below. ","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/waitaki-district-council_a-transformed-brand-for-a-transformed-activity-7365488084030799874-Nnm0"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Waitaki District Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/waitaki-district-council"},"datePublished":"2025-08-21T20:49:33.232Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/waitaki-district-council_what-is-a-locality-officer-we-have-four-activity-7364398277573693440-Ao2o","text":"What is a Locality Officer? 
We have four locality officers for the Waitaki District, and each of them lives in the area they serve. We have one locality officer for the Waihemo Ward, two for Oamaru and Corriedale, and one for the Ahuriri Ward. 
They know their area, and our community probably knows them already – all of our Locality Officers have worked at Council for a while.  
By making sure each area has someone with that local knowledge, we’re focused on providing the individual attention Waihemo, Corriedale, Oamaru and Ahuriri needs.  
We’re a big district, one size doesn’t fit all when it comes to our communities. 
They’re our people on the ground, in your community, who can help you with your enquiries out there – while working with our Case Officers to help resolve cases. 
They’ll be out there supporting the community and Council; 
 - When it needs someone to resolve the request or issue, without getting contractors involved – getting it done quickly! 
 - Gathering information, confirming details e.g. If unclear if a case is on Council, private or public land managed by another entity.     
 - Where an inspection or photographic evidence is needed. This could be abandoned vehicles, illegal parking, private overgrown vegetation blocking vision in the road corridor etc.   
 - If more information is needed before Council gets a contractor or specialist staff involved.  
 - If it’s an odd one, and the exact issue cannot be determined or does not fit with a single team’s usual scope of work – but we’ve got to do something e.g. wandering rooster not moving on from the berm of a local road occasionally flying into traffic, a possible water leak reported that also could just be a drainage issue etc.

Our staff come from all over the world (everywhere except Antarctica, in fact).

Most of our employees live in and around Oamaru and enjoy an enviable lifestyle free of gridlock traffic and pollution. Historically a food-producing region, Waitaki's food tourism market is growing, as are adventure tourism opportunities. We have beautiful lakes, tramping, fishing and hunting; and ​beaches with great surf and brilliant white sand - weekend plans here consist of asking, 'what cool thing would we like to do next?'​ 

​Oamaru is Waitaki's main town. Home to around 12,000 people, Oamaru offers the historic Victorian precinct, little blue penguins and Steampunk HQ.  There are more artists here than you can shake a stick and our residents love dressing up, having a festival, any excuse, really.

We have award-winning restaurants, wineries, craft breweries and the Whitestone Geopark's magnificent geological sites. The scenery is exquisite: spectacular mountains, shimmering lakes - we like to bike: the A2O cycle trail extends from Aoraki Mt Cook all the way to Oamaru on the eastern coast.

          <p class="break-words text-color-text" data-test-id="about-us__description">
              Waitaki District Council provides a huge range of facilities and services for a population of around 20,000 residents. 

We employ outstanding people whose skills and experience reflect our desire to provide the best for these facilities and services. They include water and roading engineers, horticulture specialists, urban planners, accountants and other financial specialists, building inspectors, public health experts, IT and software engineers, swim instructors and lifeguards, communication professionals, event co-ordinators, curators, parking officers, administrators, PAs, HR specialists, librarians, and customer service staff. Our staff come from all over the world (everywhere except Antarctica, in fact).

Most of our employees live in and around Oamaru and enjoy an enviable lifestyle free of gridlock traffic and pollution. Historically a food-producing region, Waitaki's food tourism market is growing, as are adventure tourism opportunities. We have beautiful lakes, tramping, fishing and hunting; and beaches with great surf and brilliant white sand - weekend plans here consist of asking, 'what cool thing would we like to do next?' 

Oamaru is Waitaki's main town. Home to around 12,000 people, Oamaru offers the historic Victorian precinct, little blue penguins and Steampunk HQ.  There are more artists here than you can shake a stick and our residents love dressing up, having a festival, any excuse, really.

We have award-winning restaurants, wineries, craft breweries and the Whitestone Geopark's magnificent geological sites. The scenery is exquisite: spectacular mountains, shimmering lakes - we like to bike: the A2O cycle trail extends from Aoraki Mt Cook all the way to Oamaru on the eastern coast.

What are you waiting for? Come work with us.

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">👨💻: Council shortlisted for the ALGIM project of the year award

New CitizenCentral portal in testing, to be launched later this year.

A new way for ratepayers in Waitaki to pay their rates, register their dogs, and log enquiries and requests with Council has been shortlisted for the Association of Local Government Information Management (ALGIM) project of the year award.

CitizenCentral is a customer-focused portal which ties in with Council’s existing digital infrastructure, allowing greater on-demand access to a range of Council’s services.

In just three months, the project team has set up;

• Complete 24/7 access including payment status, history, and outstanding balances.
• Integrated platform for rates, water, and infringement payments, creating and reviewing
• service requests, progress tracking, and updating citizen details.
• Multi-ratepayer payment capability from any location
• Future-ready animal registration system

The best part? The cost for this is under $30,000 – clocking in at $29,115. Instead of the expensive replacing of an entire system, this makes better use of what already works – and gives the community 24/7 access to online services.

Waitaki District Council is the first council in New Zealand to implement CitizenCentral, as part of its commitment to being a leading, innovative Council which delivers the best for the community.

CitizenCentral is the product of the new operating model for Council, bringing together Customer Services, Digital Services and the team responsible for Council’s transformation programme.

The portal itself is currently being tested by a selected group of community members, before a fuller public rollout later this year.

The winners will be announced on Wednesday, 26 November 2025.</p>

        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">✈️: Oamaru Airport welcomes new manager

As Oamaru Airports first ever full-time manager, Matt Sisson has spent his first month in the role getting to know the country’s sixth busiest airport for plane movements. 

“I don’t think people understand just how many aircraft are on the move just north of town these days” he said, “The idea that Oamaru is a sleepy little airport is definitely not the reality once you get airside. That presents challenges, and the most important one is how the airport grows sustainably and safely in the future”

With more than 14 years’ experience as an aircraft engineer at Air New Zealand, he’s no stranger to the aviation world. That hands-on technical background naturally led him into managing Airport Operations and Safety at Timaru and Hokitika Airports, where he focused on keeping things running smoothly and safely for both staff and travelers.

Matt brings close to 10 years of experience in construction project management — including leading the apron extension and runway reseal at Timaru Airport. His mix of aviation and project work means he’s got a sharp eye for detail, a strong sense of the big picture, and a practical, solution-focused mindset.

Ensuring the current runway surface life extends to the 2027/28 financial year, when the Long-Term Plan budget allocates funding for resurfacing, is also a priority.

“My role is to manage the airport, meet all of the safety and regulatory requirements and ensure that the assets owned by Council meet the planning and budgetary needs set by the Mayor and Councillors.”

Speaking about the appointment, Council Chief Executive, Alex Parmley said:

“Oamaru airport is a fantastic asset for our district and our local economy and it has grown immensely over recent years. This means there is more to do to ensure the airport runs safely, and that it is well managed and maintained, particularly with this increased use. Carrying on the way we were was not an option and we knew we needed an aviation professional with a community focus and a collaborative approach to help us manage the airport and make improvements.”

“It is great to welcome Matt to Waitaki. He’s genuinely passionate about the aviation industry and is looking forward to working alongside Council teams and the users of the airport to help deliver a safe, efficient, and community-friendly airport environment.”

Media Release:</p>

        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">🏗️: Pier pressure? Not with the Kakanui Bridge replacement.

Waitaki District Council is mid-way through replacing the 126-year-old Kakanui Bridge. Four of its piers are now in place, with two more being installed in the coming weeks. The first of the 42 bridge beams were also delivered to site this week.

This is a State Highway 1 resilience route, and by reducing the piers in the water from 15 to just 6, and raising the height of the bridge, it's designed to handle high-river flows and reduce the issues that slash buildup cause on the existing bridge.

The old bridge will be deconstructed once the new one opens, and while it's a beloved part of Kakanui - it has reached the end of its use-life (and beaten its anticipated lifespan by over a quarter century!) A new boat ramp will be built where the old bridge connects to the west bank of the Kakanui River.

This refresh also coincides with Council’s transformation into a more rationally organized, cost effective and efficient organisation – to ensure Waitaki District Council is a leading, innovative council delivering the best for our communities.

The change will be digital-first, updating assets and logos and colour palletes across our increasing online offering. Offline, we’ll be renewing signage, uniforms and fleet as part of the existing budgets for replacement.

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">What is a Locality Officer? 
We have four locality officers for the Waitaki District, and each of them lives in the area they serve. We have one locality officer for the Waihemo Ward, two for Oamaru and Corriedale, and one for the Ahuriri Ward. 
They know their area, and our community probably knows them already – all of our Locality Officers have worked at Council for a while.  
By making sure each area has someone with that local knowledge, we’re focused on providing the individual attention Waihemo, Corriedale, Oamaru and Ahuriri needs.  
We’re a big district, one size doesn’t fit all when it comes to our communities. 
They’re our people on the ground, in your community, who can help you with your enquiries out there – while working with our Case Officers to help resolve cases. 
They’ll be out there supporting the community and Council; 
 - When it needs someone to resolve the request or issue, without getting contractors involved – getting it done quickly! 
 - Gathering information, confirming details e.g. If unclear if a case is on Council, private or public land managed by another entity.     
 - Where an inspection or photographic evidence is needed. This could be abandoned vehicles, illegal parking, private overgrown vegetation blocking vision in the road corridor etc.   
 - If more information is needed before Council gets a contractor or specialist staff involved.  
 - If it’s an odd one, and the exact issue cannot be determined or does not fit with a single team’s usual scope of work – but we’ve got to do something e.g. wandering rooster not moving on from the berm of a local road occasionally flying into traffic, a possible water leak reported that also could just be a drainage issue etc. 
Our transformation involved getting more local, and with our Customer Liaison Officers, Case Officers and Locality Officers working together – we can provide a more personal, efficient service to the communities which make up Waitaki. </p>
